occupation.note: NAMED AS THE BUILDER AND NOT AS THE OCCUPANT, which is all the source says: 'The first store building on Lake Street, a two-story frame structure, was built by Thomas Church.' A man who builds a store is usually a merchant and this record reads it that way one grade down.

persons.note: THE THINNEST DOCUMENTED PERSON IN THE PARCEL AND THE RECORD SAYS SO. The whole of the evidence is one sentence in an uncredited editorial addendum at the foot of a chicagology page, which this project already grades as the weakest text in its own source set. A Thomas Church appears in Andreas's city rosters as an alderman in 1845, ten years past the scene date, which corroborates a man of that name in Chicago and dates nothing here. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 1 time, as “CHURCH THOS JR”, 1835-08-05: 1 federal land entry — W2 sec 34 T39N R13E, 160.00 acres stated in all, for $200.00 (ls0868). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: CHURCH THOS JR matches Thomas Church: the forename names Thomas Church of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

resident_research.evidence_for: Independent of the post office in books, 1840 census, civic rolls and more.
resident_research.notes: Candidate facts remain unasserted until a source bridges the candidate to the historical record by more than name similarity.

research_note: A HOUSEHOLD WRITTEN ALMOST ENTIRELY TO KEEP A BUILDING FROM BEING ANONYMOUS, and graded so that a reader can see it. Every field but the name is derived or conjectural. It is kept because an empty building on Lake Street tells a visitor less than a named man with three warnings attached.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.

address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Church, Thomas, grocery and provision store, hi Lake st'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: NOT READ BACK, BECAUSE SOMETHING BETTER ALREADY STANDS. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints an address against this name in 1839, and it is left where it is. An 1835 placement already stands: this household works at `thomas_church_store`, and clause 2 says an attested 1835 placement always beats a door printed 4 years later. The later address stays on the record as 1839's evidence and moves nothing.
